transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Congress returns next week with government funding
and military spending still on its agenda.
Republicans will have one final stretch
to act before Democrats take control
of both chambers in January.
NPR's Eric McDaniel reports the election results could complicate
that unfinished work.
>> Government funding, that runs out of money in December 11th,
so just about a month away.
They're also not going to negotiate the full suite
of 12 annual spending bills, so they'll do some kind
of kick-the-can extension, and Democrats will have to deal
with it in the new Congress.
Still, it's going to be messy.
I should also say that it's almost certain we'll see a vote
this week to impeach the Secretary of Defense,
who's upset even enough Republican lawmakers
over his lack of transparency about the war in Iran
to make that vote pretty interesting to watch.
>> That's NPR's Eric McDaniel reporting.
Russia launched another round of missiles
against the Ukrainian capital overnight.
The strikes came hours after President Philodomir Zelensky
warned that Russia was preparing another large-scale
infrastructure attack, and PR's Eleanor Beardsley reports.
>> Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said at least five people
were injured, and Kyiv's crucial northern bridge was damaged.
The first barrage of missiles came a few minutes
before 11 p.m. Residents received an all-clear signal
about 30 minutes later
before another air alert came shortly after midnight
with a fresh wave of missiles hitting the city.
Kyiv, the size of Berlin with a population of 3 million,
has come under relentless assault in recent weeks
as Russia begins its annual campaign
against Ukraine's power grid.
While Ukraine lacks air defenses now,
Russia is more easily financing its war
after the Trump administration lifted sanctions
on the sale of Russian diesel.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Krakovec, Ukraine.
>> Airlines, airports, and broadcasters across Europe
are bracing for more hoax bomb threats
following a week of flight disruptions and evacuations.
Vicky Barker reports investigators
are trying to determine who's responsible
and whether the threats are connected.
>> National and regional investigators
are trying to find out who's behind the hoaxes,
which have come amid a backdrop of cyberattacks
and drone sightings apparently designed
to disrupt civilian infrastructure and daily life.
More than two dozen commercial flights
between 16 countries
were targeted over two days this past week.
London's Heathrow Airport and Birmingham's airport
also received threats.
Then, on Friday, several media organizations in Ireland,
Bulgaria, and the UK were forced to evacuate
after emails warned of bombs in their buildings.
But whether this represented an escalation
by the original hoaxers
or was the work of separate actors isn't yet clear.
For "NPR News," I'm Vicky Barker in London.
>> This is "NPR News."
Democrats who promised to push Medicare for all
in states like Michigan, Iowa, and Maine
will now have to get the rest of their party on board.
Kate Wells with KFF Health News reports
that's not going to be an easy sell.
The idea of replacing most or all private health insurance
with a single government program,
which is what Medicare for all typically means,
Jonathan Oberlander says that is just not going to fly
in more conservative states.
He is a healthcare reform expert
at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
>> However, if Medicare for all advocates
are willing to compromise
and carve out a greater role for private insurance,
then you could draw a scenario
where you have an AOC as president,
big Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.
Is that possible? Yes.
>> But in the short term, Democrats are likely to focus
on trying to get Republican buy-in
for things like restoring tax subsidies
for some Obamacare plans.
I'm Kate Wells.
>> The Trump administration is moving ahead with plans
for a massive memorial arch,
even as a federal court temporarily blocks construction.
A website launched on Friday showcases
the proposed 250-foot structure
between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
Plans include space for events,
munitions storage, and positions for snipers.
Trump's construction and renovation projects
could face greater scrutiny
when Democrats take control of Congress in January.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Congress returns next week with government funding deadline December 11 and military spending pending
Republicans face final stretch before Democrats take control of both chambers in January
Vote expected this week to impeach Defense Secretary over lack of transparency on Iran war
Russia launches another missile barrage on Kyiv, damaging northern bridge and injuring at least five
Ukraine warns of Russian infrastructure attack as Russia targets its power grid
Trump administration lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales, easing Russia's war financing
Hoax bomb threats disrupt flights and media organizations across Europe, including Heathrow and Birmingham airports
Investigators probe whether European bomb hoaxes are connected or the work of separate actors
Democrats pushing Medicare for all in Michigan, Iowa, and Maine face resistance from party colleagues
Experts say single-payer Medicare for all unlikely in conservative states; Democrats eye restoring Obamacare subsidies
Trump administration advances massive memorial arch near Arlington despite temporary federal court block
Trump construction and renovation projects may face greater congressional scrutiny in January
